highlights.title: Run real Pi agents from your browser
highlights.summary: Create, configure and supervise agents without giving up the genuine Pi terminal.

highlights.title: Keep a fleet across projects
highlights.summary: Group agents by workspace and keep their sessions running when the browser closes.

highlights.title: Take supervision to your phone
highlights.summary: Pair a mobile browser to see running work, answer Inbox requests and open terminals.

highlights.title: Matrix: your agents and terminals on one canvas
highlights.summary: Open a matrix and watch several agents, terminals, notes, files and diffs live side by side. Pan and zoom a plane that holds as many as you need.

highlights.title: Zoom out and nothing stops working
highlights.summary: Panels you are not reading show their last screen instead of a live one, so a big matrix costs only the terminals you are actually watching.

highlights.title: A managed agent's panel is its conversation
highlights.summary: Follow a turn as it streams, and see at a glance which agent is waiting on you — even zoomed out, where a panel is only a name-plate.

highlights.title: Sessions can message each other
highlights.summary: Agents and CLI terminals send each other messages through PiCode, with a durable inbox, explicit acknowledgement and your own view of every conversation.

highlights.title: Link two panels to pair two sessions
highlights.summary: Drag a connector between two panels and those sessions become contacts, even across project folders. The link never shares a transcript, and removing it removes the permission.

highlights.title: Fullscreen for any tab
highlights.summary: Give a terminal, a matrix or an editor the whole window. The sidebar and tabs come back when the pointer touches an edge.

highlights.title: Pins became notes that come back
highlights.summary: Search, keep on top, archive, and set a reminder that files itself into your Inbox when it is due — on the desktop and on the phone.

highlights.title: The git graph acts on what you point at
highlights.summary: Right-click a commit, a branch or a worktree to prepare the exact command in a terminal, or ask an agent working in that folder to run it.

highlights.title: Local llama.cpp, managed
highlights.summary: Install, run and watch a local llama.cpp service from PiCode, with download progress and a health view of its own.

highlights.title: One tray icon on Windows
highlights.summary: The shell is now the only resident: close its window and the service keeps running in the tray; reopen and you are back where you were.

highlights.title: The work browser grew up
highlights.summary: Site permissions, downloads, history, autofill and one-click clear — the built-in browser now covers daily work.

highlights.title: Muse Code and Antigravity join Agent CLIs
highlights.summary: Launch them from the catalog, browse their sessions, and hand a conversation to another CLI with Continue in….

highlights.title: Agents can read the page you are on
highlights.summary: A new browser tool plus act-tier grants: an agent can read the open page and, when you allow it, act on it.

highlights.title: Text and polish on the canvas
highlights.summary: Drop text anywhere on the plane, right-click for its own menu, and read the zoom level at a glance.

highlights.title: Snippets everywhere, including the phone
highlights.summary: Save reusable prompts and commands once; write, duplicate and archive them from the desk or the phone.

highlights.title: The tray reopens the shell
highlights.summary: Closing the window hid it for good; tray click and Open PiCode now bring it back on the same page.

highlights.title: No more stray console window
highlights.summary: The shell no longer opens a terminal window next to its tray icon on every start.

highlights.title: Every agent CLI, managed like Pi was
highlights.summary: Claude Code, Codex, Grok, Hermes, OpenCode, Muse Code, Antigravity and Omp each get a real Settings, Memory, Packages and Providers pane that edits the CLI's own files — the vendor's own keys, named as the vendor names them.

highlights.title: One vault for every sign-in
highlights.summary: See which accounts this machine holds, import the login a CLI already has, add an API key, verify it or sign out. One account per provider or ten, encrypted at rest.

highlights.title: PiCode's own tools reach the other CLIs
highlights.summary: Inbox, Checklist, Browser and Computer now serve over MCP with the same names and answers the pi packages give, switchable per launch.

highlights.title: Any script can ask you a question and wait
highlights.summary: `picode inbox ask --question "…" --wait` files the question in your Inbox and blocks until you answer — hours if needed — then prints your reply. No MCP configuration.

highlights.title: An agent can drive the desktop
highlights.summary: Switch Computer on for one agent and it can see the screen, click, type, use the clipboard and open programs with your permissions. Every call, allowed or refused, is listed. Off by default.

highlights.title: Know what is listening, and stop it
highlights.summary: The Inspector's Servers tab names what each port actually answered, who started it and how long it has been up — and offers Open, Show terminal and Stop for the ones PiCode can attribute.

highlights.title: Web apps keep their own logins
highlights.summary: Each installed web app has its own session store, so a second account of the same service is a second tile — and either can be cleared or forgotten on its own.

highlights.title: The Inspector came to the phone
highlights.summary: Changes, Files and the diff view now open on mobile, and Changes follows a dirty linked worktree instead of describing the wrong checkout.

highlights.title: Windows setup finishes on a clean machine
highlights.summary: `picode-desktop install` now delivers the Linux binary and the runtime — tmux, git, curl, Node.js — so a fresh Windows box reaches a working PiCode without a manual WSL session.

highlights.title: One packages pane, every CLI
highlights.summary: Nine agent CLIs share one Packages pane: install, update, enable, disable or remove from a single list that names each entry's CLI and scope, and offers only the controls that CLI can actually honour.

highlights.title: An agent can carry its own packages
highlights.summary: Pi and Omp agents take packages at agent scope — the entry rides that one agent's next start, so an extension loads for a single agent instead of the whole fleet.

highlights.title: Omp's own extensions are on the page
highlights.summary: The extensions Omp loads at start now appear in the pane, with a working enable and disable that edits Omp's own list of disabled extensions and leaves every other byte alone.

highlights.title: Key maps are editable on four more CLIs
highlights.summary: Omp, Codex, OpenCode and Antigravity key bindings open in PiCode's Settings pane, editing the CLI's own file rather than a copy.

highlights.title: Omp's model roles, edited where they live
highlights.summary: Every role Omp has — plus any you invented — gets a row with a model picker fed by Omp itself, fallback chains as ordered lists, and the quick-switch cycle, on both layers including the workspace file `omp config set` cannot reach.

highlights.title: A project can declare how it integrates
highlights.summary: Delivery reads a workspace's own declaration — fast-forward only, plus up to eight single-line commands — and an agent can request a place in that queue and step back out, with the owner ordering and authorizing entries. The executor that runs them is still to come.

highlights.title: Automations reach agents of other CLIs
highlights.summary: A scheduled or webhook message to a Claude Code, Codex or Omp agent is pasted into that agent's terminal while it is open, and a closed terminal says so in the Inbox instead of giving another reason.

highlights.title: The panes follow the agent you are on
highlights.summary: Settings, Packages, Providers and Connectors open the CLI of the selected agent instead of always Pi, from the user menu or the Ctrl+K palette.

highlights.title: Setup asks for less
highlights.summary: Getting started installs tmux and PiCode first, the picker lists a CLI only when it is installed, and PiCode Desktop on Windows brings the runtime — tmux, git, curl, Node.js and npm — without choosing an agent CLI for you.

highlights.title: Removing an agent asks how it went
highlights.summary: The remove dialog, on the desktop and the phone, asks one optional question — Resolved, Partly, Didn't resolve, Just trying — and, when it did not go well, what got in the way. It never blocks Remove, and the Outcomes page keeps every answer with what PiCode saw: how long it lived, its turns, how often it asked for you.

highlights.title: Landing rules you can read and edit
highlights.summary: A machine's rules for landing delivered work — fast-forward only, plus up to eight checks — are now a Preferences page that names which workspaces follow them, with per-workspace rules and an Edit shortcut; the same page exists on the phone.

highlights.title: An authorized entry actually runs
highlights.summary: Authorizing a queue entry is execution authority now: PiCode runs the operation the project declared and records on the entry what it did, or the reason it did not — one operation per repository, with every stale authorization a named blocker rather than a silent move.

highlights.title: Spend stops guessing
highlights.summary: Claude Code, Codex and Grok tokens are counted once (the dashboard was showing roughly double for two of them), Claude Code subagents count, and a CLI whose turns carry no price is estimated at list price — marked as an estimate, and a CLI's own figure always wins.

highlights.title: Backups cover every agent CLI
highlights.summary: A snapshot keeps each CLI's settings, its login file with Include secrets, and the conversations of Claude Code, Codex, Grok, Omp and Muse Code as well as Pi's; restore puts them back. OpenCode, Hermes and Antigravity keep conversations in a live database, which is not copied.

highlights.title: Ways out of PiCode, from the workspace menu
highlights.summary: Show the folder in Explorer, copy its path, open the repository on GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket or Azure DevOps, and open or create the pull request for the current branch.

highlights.title: Omp's models and roles in one pane
highlights.summary: Every model Omp reports it can reach, and the role map — roles, fallback chains, the quick-switch cycle, thinking levels — edited where they live, including the workspace file `omp config set` cannot reach.

highlights.title: Terminals that lied are gone
highlights.summary: A terminal whose shell was already dead no longer survives as an empty row, and creating one right after closing the last no longer fails when tmux's server had just emptied.

highlights.title: A fleet's settings keep up
highlights.summary: Workspace settings from the card's menu, Checks and tool approval in Omp's Settings, a Limits card that shows every plan PiCode can read, and `/login` opening where you are looking.
